items.title: Add opt-in structured errors for Guardian circuit-breaker interruptions
items.body:
Add opt-in structured errors for Guardian circuit-breaker interruptions

## Why

Guardian denial-limit interruptions lack a structured error identifying the cause. Make this opt-in because older clients may not recognize the new error in shared history.

## What changed

- Add `auto_review.circuit_break_action = "strict"` to attach `TooManyDenials` to the interrupted turn. The default leaves the error unset.
- Expose `turn.error.codexErrorInfo = "tooManyDenials"` in app-server notifications and saved history, and update protocol schemas and generated types.
- Preserve the warning, denial limit, and interrupted status without emitting a separate error notification.

## Testing

Add an integration test covering omitted, `default`, and `strict` settings, checking warnings, live turn errors, the absence of separate error notifications, and persisted turn errors after restart.

### What version of the IDE extension are you using?

26.917.62051

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro

### Which IDE are you using?

VS Code: 1.139.1, user setup, VS Code commit: 04c0d99f4fb0d8afe6ce4f0c58e31e183ac3e4b1

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 Enterprise, x64, build 26100

### What issue are you seeing?

In an ongoing Codex chat in VS Code, an assistant progress report was initially visible, then appeared to disappear. I found it behind a `>` disclosure on a command/activity entry. Clicking `>` revealed the report, but the disclosure control was no longer visible afterward, so I could not collapse it again.



### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Continue an existing Codex chat containing assistant reports and command/activity entries.
2. An assistant report appears in the chat.
3. The report later appears to be missing.
4. Click the `>` disclosure on an activity entry; the report becomes visible.
5. Look for the control to collapse the entry; it is no longer visible.

This was observed in a long-running chat. I do not yet have a guaranteed reproduction sequence.


### What is the expected behavior?

Assistant reports remain visible as assistant messages. If an activity disclosure can contain a report, its expand/collapse control remains available in both states.



### Observed behavior

The report appeared to vanish until I expanded an activity entry. Once expanded, the `>` control disappeared. I could read the report but could not collapse that entry again.

### Environment

- VS Code commit: 04c0d99f4fb0d8afe6ce4f0c58e31e183ac3e4b1
- Chromium: 150.0.7871.250

### Related issues

- #9646 — related VS Code disclosure/control visibility behavior
- #23221 — related assistant-response visibility inside a collapsed activity block

These appear related, but I am reporting the observed expand-then-missing-control sequence separately.

### Additional evidence

Observed at approximately September 27, 2026, 4:35 p.m. CDT.

items.title: [macOS] Cannot drag-select message text; double-click word selection still works

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
## Summary

In a Codex session in the ChatGPT desktop app on macOS, I cannot select a range of message text by dragging. Double-clicking a word still highlights that word, but I cannot extend the selection across words or lines.

This has happened more than once. Text selection in the message composer works; the failure affects rendered conversation messages.

## Environment

- App: ChatGPT desktop, using a Codex session
- App version: `26.924.22138` (build `11645`), verified from the running app's installed bundle
- macOS: `27.0` (build `26A428`)
- Observed: September 27, 2026

## Steps to reproduce while the issue is present

1. Open a conversation containing rendered message text.
2. Click and drag across several words or lines in a message.
3. Observe that the intended text range is not selected.
4. Double-click a word in the message. That single word becomes highlighted.
5. Try extending the selection by double-clicking and holding the second click while dragging, or by clicking a starting point and Shift-clicking an endpoint. Neither method extends the highlight beyond a word.
6. Compare with selection in the message composer, where selection works.

The trigger that puts the conversation into this state is unknown. This is a recurring problem, but I have not established whether it affects every conversation or only particular sessions.

## Expected behavior

Clicking and dragging over rendered message text should select a continuous range across words and lines for copying.

## Actual behavior

Single-word selection by double-click works, but selecting a longer passage or extending the selection fails. Composer selection is unaffected.

## Troubleshooting and evidence limits

- Double-click word selection: works.
- Ordinary drag selection in messages: fails.
- Double-click-and-drag to extend selection: fails.
- Shift-click to extend selection: fails.
- Selection in the composer: works.
- Whether restarting the app resolves the issue has not yet been established.
- No root cause or renderer failure has been verified.

## Related reports

- #40468: macOS renderer crash when copying or starting a drag on selected message text. It also describes double-click word selection working and composer selection being unaffected, but its reported outcome is a crash.
- #38862: severe slowdown when drag-selecting assistant response text on macOS.

These may concern related interactions, but neither is a confirmed duplicate of this report. The symptom here is that message-text selection cannot be extended beyond a single word.

items.body:
## Summary
Codex desktop used avoidably large browser observations, repeated checks and prolonged retries while configuring one form. The session had explicit instructions to retrieve narrowly, stop and reassess after two failures, and avoid unnecessary repeated verification, but the agent did not consistently follow them.

## Environment
- macOS, Codex desktop
- Configured model: gpt-6-astra; reasoning effort: high
- Browser interaction through the computer-use tool with accessibility snapshots and scoped DOM reads
- Observed on 27 September 2026
- Exact application build and wasted-token total have not been measured

## Task and observed behaviour
The user asked the agent to update a single enterprise web form, populate three read-only fields, and add an information section matching an existing form.

1. The agent repeatedly retrieved large accessibility snapshots containing substantial unrelated form data instead of only the affected fields or controls.
2. It repeatedly read state and retried actions during slow UI postbacks; some observations returned unchanged state. These sequences substantially expanded the conversation.
3. When the web editor rejected HTML formatting, the agent continued troubleshooting and saved an unformatted fallback that did not meet the requested model. The user had to reject the formatting.
4. The useful handoff was eventually a plain-text file containing literal HTML tags, but this was reached after avoidable rework.
5. When challenged about efficiency, the agent initially suggested starting separate tasks at deliverable boundaries. The user pointed out that this was one form; the agent then acknowledged that the problem was its execution, not task scope.

## Expected behaviour

items.title: [Pets][Diagnostics] Simple custom-pet sprite defects can trigger excessive agent investigation and usage-window burn

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: model-behavior
labels.description: Issues related to behaviors exhibited by the model

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Windows Store package: `OpenAI.Codex_26.924.2738.0_x64__2p2nqsd0c76g0`

### What subscription do you have?

Plus / paid usage window affected

### What platform is your computer?

Windows desktop

### What issue are you seeing?

This is both a **pet/custom-avatar bug report** and a **complaint about model/runtime efficiency**.

A local custom pet had a simple visual defect in its idle animation: the final idle frame was off-center and clipped the tail feathers. The eventual working fix was trivial: replace the bad idle frame with a good one.

However, diagnosing this consumed roughly **80–90% of a 5-hour model/runtime window**. The agent escalated through cache theories, process inspection, renderer/window tracing, packaged app internals, `app.asar` inspection, sprite contract discovery, and other deep diagnostics before the obvious artifact-level fix was tried.

That is far too expensive for this class of problem.

There are two parts:

1. **Product bug / usability problem:** the pet renderer provides no lightweight way to inspect the active sprite/animation/frame, making a simple custom-pet frame defect hard to diagnose.
2. **Efficiency complaint:** a visually local problem should not casually burn most of a multi-hour usage window before basic artifact inspection is attempted.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Install and select a local custom pet.
2. Use a valid V2 spritesheet.
3. Observe the pet’s idle animation.
4. In this case, the final idle frame appeared shifted/off-center and clipped the tail feathers.
5. The current product surface provides no quick way to identify the exact active frame, exact rendered spritesheet bytes, fixed cell bounds, or whether visible content exceeds a frame cell.

### What is the expected behavior?

For pet/custom-avatar bugs, there should be a cheap, bounded, **artifact-first** diagnostic path before any deep runtime investigation.

At minimum, a read-only **Pet Doctor / Avatar Diagnostics** surface should expose:

- active pet ID and display name
- exact spritesheet path currently in use
- sprite version
- sheet dimensions
- cell dimensions
- active animation
- active row/frame
- current asset hash
- whether rendered bytes match the current on-disk file
- per-frame alpha/content bounds
- whether a frame touches or exceeds its cell boundaries

Ideally it would also show the active animation as a strip of frames with cell boundaries overlaid.

Expected troubleshooting order:

1. inspect the actual visual asset/frame
2. test the smallest local fix
3. only escalate into cache/process/renderer internals if that fails

### What is the actual behavior?

Troubleshooting escalated through:

- cache analysis
- process inspection
- window enumeration
- packaged app inspection
- `app.asar` search
- renderer contract discovery

The practical fix was simply:

> the last idle frame was visibly wrong; replacing frame 6 with frame 1 fixed the clipping.

### Additional information

Relevant technical findings:

- The local custom pet was selected successfully.
- The app **was** loading the current local atlas from disk.
- The issue was **not** caused by stale cache.
- V2 sheet size: `1536x2288`.
- Cell size: `192x208`.
- Grid: `8 columns x 11 rows`.
- Idle uses row 0.
- The visible problem was in the final idle frame.
- Replacing the last idle frame with the first idle frame fixed the clipping locally.
- This fix is local-only and does not automatically sync to any cloud/source version of the pet asset.

### Cross-agent handoff failure

There was also a second, important failure mode: **an unsupported hypothesis was promoted into a fact and then handed to the next agent as the premise of the investigation.**

The first/smaller model:

- identified the final idle frame as the likely visual problem;
- shifted that frame approximately 6 px left;
- immediately reported the issue as fixed before the visual result had actually been verified;
- when the clipping persisted, reclassified the problem as a **stale animation/cache** problem;
- deselected/reselected the pet, relaunched the app, cleared Chromium-related caches, and at one point used a relaunch path that triggered a Windows package-identity error;
- then produced a handoff prompt stating that Windows “keeps rendering the previous atlas” even though that had not been established.

The subsequent agent inherited that statement as if it were an observation rather than a hypothesis. It then spent substantial additional runtime trying to locate the supposed persistence/cache layer.

A later reversible visual-marker test proved that the desktop app was in fact rendering the **current local atlas bytes**, which invalidated the stale-atlas premise.

The final fix came from simply inspecting all six idle cells visually: frame 6 itself was still bad/off-center, so replacing frame 6 with frame 1 fixed the clipping.

This suggests agent handoffs should explicitly separate:

- **observations** — what has actually been verified;
- **hypotheses** — what might explain those observations;
- **attempted fixes** — what was changed;
- **verification status** — whether the attempted fix was actually confirmed.

A handoff such as “Windows keeps rendering the previous atlas” should not be emitted unless stale bytes have actually been demonstrated. A safer handoff would have been: “The visible pet still clips after modifying frame 6; it is not yet established whether the renderer is using stale bytes or whether the modified frame itself is still defective.”

That distinction would likely have prevented a large amount of unnecessary downstream investigation.

### Impact

A problem equivalent to a malformed single frame / a few-pixel alignment issue consumed roughly **80–90% of a 5-hour usage window**.

Please consider:

1. adding a **Pet Doctor / Avatar Diagnostics** runtime;
2. making pet troubleshooting **artifact-first**;
3. improving **budget awareness** so local visual bugs do not trigger hours of infrastructure archaeology before simple frame inspection is attempted;
4. making cross-agent handoffs preserve **observations vs. hypotheses vs. verification status** so one model’s speculative diagnosis does not become the next model’s assumed fact.

### What issue are you seeing?

In a Desktop-managed Remote SSH task backed by a Mac, the built-in browser panel visibly loads pages and ambient browser context reaches the task, but the supported browser-control API cannot discover or select the IAB backend.

A separate desktop-local task on the same physical Mac successfully opened example.com in IAB, clicked Learn more, and reached IANA with the title Example Domains. This was a diagnostic comparison; moving production work to local projects is not an acceptable workaround.

The user reports that browser use previously worked while using remote projects, which are their normal workflow. The last known-good version and whether the earlier successful path was specifically IAB versus Chrome have not been established. Please investigate a possible regression or configuration/connection mismatch rather than assuming that remote browser use was never supported.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Run the macOS desktop app and use a saved Remote SSH project backed by a Mac with the app and bundled runtime installed.
2. Continue an ordinary SSH-backed task. In our reproduction, the desktop app is also running on the execution Mac and its panel for the affected task is visible there.
3. Open example.com in that task's built-in browser panel.
4. Ask the task to use the built-in browser, click Learn more, and report the resulting title.
5. Observe that supported browser discovery lists Chrome only and selecting `iab` fails.
6. Check desktop logs at the same instant: native browser-pipe peer authorization rejects the connection.
7. As a comparison only, run the same navigation in a new desktop-local task on that Mac; it succeeds.

The current failure has been reproduced repeatedly in this existing remote task. A fresh remote-task reproduction has not yet been established.

### What is the expected behavior?

The remote task should be able to control its authorized built-in browser while shell/filesystem work remains on the remote host, preserving session ownership and security checks. If this exact topology requires different supported setup, provide the concrete configuration/recovery procedure and an actionable error.

Do not require switching project work to local tasks or disabling native peer authorization.

Sanitized, time-correlated evidence from the most recent discovery request:

> 2026-09-27T21:08:31.879Z warning [browser-use-native-pipe-server] browser-use native pipe rejected socket peer reason=untrusted-process-ancestry

This appeared three times at that timestamp. Earlier IAB selection/discovery requests also coincided with the same rejection.

Process topology:
- The successful local task's runtime descends from the desktop-owned app-server.
- The affected remote task's runtime descends from the SSH app-server, which is detached with parent PID 1.
- Both servers use the app-bundled Codex executable.
- The running desktop executable, remote Codex executable and loaded native browser peer-authorizer match the installed files by inode, so those processes are not retaining replaced binaries from an earlier installation.
- The installed desktop, Codex, node and node_repl executables report OpenAI code-signing authority.

We have identified the failing authorization boundary, not the full root cause or the native validator's intended ancestry contract.

Earlier stale per-thread website denials were removed with user authorization, restoring Chrome access. IAB discovery still fails. Browser-runtime reset did not repair it. Full CDP remains disabled. No executable patch, security-check bypass, alternate transport, or project migration was performed. No shared-service restart was attempted during this final isolation pass because other work was active.

Related reports reviewed:
- #22844 — same Remote SSH visible-panel / unavailable-IAB symptom, including a macOS reproduction.
- #34263 — remote browser runtime provisioning; our runtime is present and Chrome works.
- #44782 — remote-host GUI route registration; our affected task's host-side panel is already open.
- #47270 — broader routing failures; a comment on build 11645 also reports native-pipe ancestry rejection.

Please determine whether this is the same underlying defect or a distinct macOS peer-authorization incompatibility with the SSH app-server lifecycle. We can provide further targeted diagnostics privately. This report intentionally omits private project names, account data, hostnames, task identifiers, browser profile data and full logs.

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

codex-cli 0.157.1 (npm), managed daemon package 0.157.1-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc

### What subscription do you have?

n/a

### Which model were you using?

gpt-6-sol

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 Pro 10.0.22631

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

Codex was launched inside a ConPTY by a session-management tool (a Go program driving `codex` through a pseudoconsole). Later sessions were plain Windows Terminal.

### Codex doctor report

```
Codex Doctor v0.157.1 · windows-x86_64
  ✓ runtime      npm, version 0.157.1, executable ...\@openai\codex-win32-x64\vendor\x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\bin\codex.exe
  ✓ install      consistent
  ⚠ sandbox      filesystem unrestricted · network enabled
```

### What issue are you seeing?

Two related problems with the shared app-server daemon on Windows. The console popups themselves are already tracked in #44768, #48440, #48422 and #48356, so this report is about the two things those don't cover.

**1. The daemon permanently keeps the environment of whichever process first launched it, and hands it to every later session.**

`daemon_auto_start` is on by default in 0.157.1, so the first interactive `codex` launch after the update installs and starts the daemon. In my case that first launch happened inside a tool that runs `codex` in a ConPTY and marks the environment of everything it starts (a `*_THREAD_ID` variable, a daemon-directory variable). The daemon is spawned with `DETACHED_PROCESS | CREATE_BREAKAWAY_FROM_JOB` (`app-server-daemon/src/backend/pid_start.rs`) and the launcher's full environment. It escaped the launcher's job, the launcher exited, and the daemon lived on.

Reading the daemon's environment block confirms it still carries the launcher's marker variables. Since every later `codex` session from any terminal attaches to this daemon, every shell command those sessions run, and every MCP server the daemon starts, now inherits the first launcher's environment instead of the environment of the terminal the user actually typed `codex` in. In my case that made the launching tool believe those later processes were running inside one of its own sessions.

Expected: the daemon should either start with a minimal environment, or per-session process spawns should use the attaching client's environment, not the daemon's.

**2. `daemon_auto_start = false` does not stop Codex from using a daemon that is already running.**

In `tui/src/startup_orchestration.rs`, `auto_start_daemon` honors `Feature::DaemonAutoStart`, but `reuse_implicit_local_daemon = daemon_exclusion.is_none()` does not. `daemon_startup::exclusion` only considers `--no-daemon`, `--oss`, `--profile`, overrides and so on. So with the feature disabled in config.toml, `maybe_probe_default_daemon_socket` still finds a live socket and the TUI attaches with `allow_embedded_fallback: true`.

Result: a user who disables the feature to avoid the Windows console popups still gets them until they also find and run `codex app-server daemon stop`, and again the next time anything (an IDE, a script, `codex app-server daemon start`) brings a daemon up. Only the per-invocation `--no-daemon` flag actually guarantees embedded mode, which the `--help` text confirms ("even if it is already running").

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Problem 1:
1. Make sure no daemon is running: `codex app-server daemon stop`.
2. From a shell, `set MY_MARKER=from-first-launcher` then run `codex`. Exit codex. The daemon stays up.
3. From a different terminal without `MY_MARKER`, run `codex` and ask it to run `cmd /c echo %MY_MARKER%` (or `echo $env:MY_MARKER`).
4. The command prints `from-first-launcher`.

Problem 2:
1. With a daemon running, add `[features] daemon_auto_start = false` to config.toml (or `codex features disable daemon_auto_start`).
2. Run `codex`. The process tree shows the new session attached to the existing daemon (the `codex.exe app-server --listen unix:// --managed-daemon` process spawns its tool processes), and the Windows console popups from the linked issues continue.
3. Run `codex --no-daemon` instead. Everything runs embedded and the popups stop.

### What is the expected behavior?

- A shared daemon should not pin one launcher's environment onto every future session.
- `daemon_auto_start = false` should mean "do not use the shared daemon", including not attaching to one that already exists, or the feature should be documented as start-only and a config-level equivalent of `--no-daemon` provided.

### Additional information

- `core/src/spawn.rs` `spawn_child_async` still sets no `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` on Windows on current `main`, which is why a console-less daemon pops a window for every shell command. Mentioned only for cross-reference with #44768.
- Verified the daemon has no console at all: `AttachConsole(daemon_pid)` fails with `ERROR_INVALID_HANDLE`, while the daemon's MCP children (spawned with `CREATE_NO_WINDOW` in `rmcp-client`) do have hidden consoles.

items.title: Codex Cloud tasks do not expose GitHub connector read tools; only make_pr is available

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: codex-web
labels.description: Issues related to Codex Web

labels.name: agent
labels.description: Issues related to the core agent loop

items.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

Codex Cloud web tasks can check out and work on a private GitHub repository through the ChatGPT Codex Connector, but the task runtime does **not expose GitHub read tools** for repositories, issues, pull requests, comments, or CI.

In affected sessions, Codex reports that the only GitHub-related capability available is `make_pr` for pull-request metadata. There is no GitHub connector/tool for reading issues or comments.

This makes repository workflows such as the following impossible in a normal Codex Cloud task:

- read the issue that defines the implementation task;
- inspect related/open issues before changing code;
- inspect existing pull requests and review comments;
- inspect CI/check results;
- compare an implementation against issue discussion/history.

The repository checkout itself works correctly. Codex can read repository files such as `AGENTS.md`, modify files, and run local commands. The missing capability is specifically the authenticated GitHub connector/tool surface inside the cloud task.

### Environment / account setup

- Codex Cloud / Codex Web
- ChatGPT Plus
- GitHub account is connected to ChatGPT/Codex
- "ChatGPT Codex Connector" GitHub App is installed
- GitHub App access is configured for all repositories
- GitHub App has read/write permissions for code, issues, pull requests, actions, and workflows
- The private repository is available in Codex Cloud and can be checked out successfully

### Steps to reproduce

1. Connect GitHub to ChatGPT/Codex.
2. Install/authorize the ChatGPT Codex Connector GitHub App for a private repository (or all repositories).
3. Create a Codex Cloud environment/task for that repository.
4. Start a **new** Codex Cloud task.
5. Ask:
   > List all open issues in the current repository using the connected GitHub connector. Do not use shell, curl, gh, or unauthenticated web access.
6. Codex responds that no GitHub connector for repository/issue queries is available and that only `make_pr` is present.
7. Ask it to inspect a specific GitHub issue or pull request and its comments using the connector.
8. The same limitation is reported.

Representative response from Codex:

> The GitHub connector is not available in this session; only a connector for creating pull-request metadata is attached. Therefore I cannot reliably list the repository's open issues through the requested GitHub connector.

### Troubleshooting already performed

- Disconnected the GitHub connection from ChatGPT/Codex.
- Reconnected and re-authorized the GitHub account.
- Verified the GitHub App installation and repository permissions.
- Reloaded Codex.
- Started completely new Codex Cloud tasks/sessions after reconnecting.
- Repeated the minimal issue-listing test.

The behavior is unchanged.

I deliberately did **not** work around this by injecting a PAT, using `gh auth login`, or exposing GitHub credentials to the cloud shell. The expected model is that the already-authorized GitHub connector is exposed as a mediated tool to the Codex agent.

### Expected behavior

A Codex Cloud task attached to a repository through the authorized GitHub connector should expose the relevant authenticated GitHub tools to the agent, at minimum read access needed to inspect:

- repository metadata;
- issues and issue comments;
- pull requests and review comments;
- CI/check/workflow status.

The shell/container does not need direct access to OAuth credentials. The GitHub connector can remain a separately mediated tool capability.

This would support a normal issue-driven development workflow such as:

1. Read the issue and discussion.
2. Read `AGENTS.md` / repository instructions and relevant code.
3. Inspect related issues/PRs to avoid conflicting work.
4. Implement and test.
5. Inspect CI/review feedback.
6. Prepare or update the PR.

### Actual behavior

The repository is successfully available to the Codex Cloud task, but authenticated GitHub read/query tools are absent from the session. Only `make_pr` is exposed.

As a result, Codex can modify the codebase but cannot independently read the GitHub issue/PR context that defines or surrounds the work.

### Why this appears to be tool provisioning rather than GitHub authorization

The same GitHub account/app authorization is valid and the repository checkout works. Re-authorizing the connection and creating new sessions does not change the available tool inventory.

The failure also occurs **before** any GitHub API request through an authenticated connector can be attempted: there simply is no issue/PR read tool exposed to the task.

### Related issues

- #38821 — Codex Cloud delegated tasks do not expose connected app/connector tools (e.g. Google Drive)
- #47839 — Codex connected apps are installed but their callable tools are not exposed to the runtime (Desktop)

Those reports appear related at the tool-injection layer, but this report is specifically about the **GitHub connector in Codex Cloud/Web**, where repository checkout works while GitHub issue/PR read tools are absent.

### Additional information

If this is an intentional limitation of Codex Cloud rather than a bug, the UI/documentation should make the boundary explicit. Today the GitHub App can be fully authorized and the repository can be selected for Codex Cloud, which strongly suggests that issue/PR-aware workflows should be available to the agent.

I can provide the exact Codex task transcript or additional diagnostics if maintainers indicate which identifiers/logs are useful.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Codex app 26.924.22138, build 11645, release channel prod

### What subscription do you have?

Unknown / not visible to this Codex task

### What platform is your computer?

Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

Codex-managed worktrees are not reliably writable by the chat/task that owns them under a permission-profile setup. This blocks normal Git development because ordinary write, stage, and commit workflows require escalation even when managed worktree metadata records the current chat as owner.

Feedback ID: 01a0e3f5-4d07-75a2-bbf4-1a2529a236be

A managed worktree created and attached to the current chat was not writable by that same chat:

```text
/Users/davise/.codex/worktrees/owner-worktree-permission-test/MN15-Discovery
```

Owner metadata:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "ownerThreadId": "01a0e3f5-4d07-75a2-bbf4-1a2529a236be"
}
```

Ordinary write from the owning chat failed:

```text
PermissionError: [Errno 1] Operation not permitted:
'/Users/davise/.codex/worktrees/owner-worktree-permission-test/MN15-Discovery/.owner_write_probe_20260927'
```

Git status was readable, but the worktree came up detached:

```text
## HEAD (no branch)
```

`git symbolic-ref --short HEAD` failed:

```text
fatal: ref HEAD is not a symbolic ref
```

Earlier, another managed worktree at `/Users/davise/.codex/worktrees/ripcord-guard-import/MN15-Discovery` was correctly branch-attached, but ordinary writes from the active task still failed with Operation not permitted. A narrow escalated write/read/remove probe to the same path succeeded, indicating the path is writable by the user account and the failure is in the task sandbox/writable-root lifecycle, not filesystem immutability or Git corruption.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Feedback ID: 01a0e3f5-4d07-75a2-bbf4-1a2529a236be

### What is the expected behavior?

When Codex creates, restores, attaches, or hands off a managed worktree for a chat, that exact task-owned checkout should be included in the task's effective writable roots. The corresponding Git metadata path needed for normal Git operations should also be available to that task.

The permission grant should be owner-specific: it should not make all sibling managed worktrees under `$CODEX_HOME/worktrees` casually writable. Protected project-path rules should still apply inside the managed worktree.

### Additional information

A candidate local workaround was tested and rejected:

```toml
[permissions.projects-contained.workspace_roots]
"/Users/davise/.codex/worktrees" = true
```

That is too broad because it may make all managed worktrees writable. It does not prove owner isolation across sibling managed worktrees, and it does not prove protected project-path rules are preserved inside nested managed worktree checkouts. The patch was rolled back.

Required fix: Codex should inject the exact owned managed worktree path, and the exact Git metadata path needed for that worktree, into the owning task's writable roots during managed-worktree lifecycle events: create, restore, attach, and handoff.

Verification criteria:
1. Fresh task in a managed worktree can create and remove a small file in its own worktree root without escalation.
2. Same task can run `git status`, `git diff`, `git add`, and `git commit` without escalation for ordinary project files.
3. Same task cannot write a sibling task's managed worktree.
4. Same task cannot write protected paths inside its managed worktree unless a protected update is explicitly authorized.
5. The fix does not require adding the entire `$CODEX_HOME/worktrees` tree as a broad writable root.

Related open issues that look relevant: #18448, #35260, #19786, #27418, #32880.

Attempting to archive the disposable same-chat test worktree through the Codex app returned: This worktree is protected by a pinned task or workspace. So the failed same-chat test worktree remains in place as current evidence.

## Issue

Archiving an existing local Codex conversation from the sidebar fails. The thread remains active instead of moving to the archived list.

The current failure is **not** the older `os error 2` failure from #39130. The current build returns Win32 `os error 183`:

```text
failed to archive session: thread-store internal error:
failed to archive thread: 当文件已存在时，无法创建该文件。 (os error 183)
```

English meaning: **Cannot create a file when that file already exists.**

The app-server response is JSON-RPC `-32603` for `thread/archive`.

The failure was triggered from the normal sidebar context-menu archive action:

```text
Archive requested ... source=sidebar_context_menu
... errorCode=-32603 ... method=thread/archive
Request failed ... "failed to archive session: thread-store internal error:
failed to archive thread: 当文件已存在时，无法创建该文件。 (os error 183)"
```

The same `os error 183` archive failure appears repeatedly in the local Desktop logs on:

- 2026-09-20
- 2026-09-22
- 2026-09-26
- 2026-09-27

The most recent captured failure occurred at `2026-09-27T03:16:00Z`.

- the active rollout JSONL still exists under `~/.codex/sessions/...`

The selected conversation should archive successfully, disappear from the active conversation list, and remain available in the archived view.

Earlier Windows archive failures were tracked in #39130 / #39150. That issue family involved `os error 2` / Windows verbatim rollout paths and was reported fixed in Desktop `26.818.3698.0` with app-server `0.149.0`.

### What version of the Codex App are you using?

Microsoft Store package `OpenAI.Codex` version `26.924.2738.0`; desktop logs report build `11645`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not included; this report concerns local MCP launch configuration.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 Home 25H2, build `26200.9457`, x64.

### What issue are you seeing?

An enabled `[mcp_servers.codex_app]` entry in `%USERPROFILE%/.codex/config.toml` referenced the versioned plugin cache directory `codex-app-tools/0.1.4`, while only `0.1.5` remained installed. This left the configured working directory pointing to a nonexistent location.

The configuration was repaired by changing only the version in `cwd`:

```diff
 [mcp_servers.codex_app]
 command = "cmd.exe"
-cwd = "C:/Users/<USER>/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-bundled/codex-app-tools/0.1.4"
+cwd = "C:/Users/<USER>/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-bundled/codex-app-tools/0.1.5"
 args = ["/d", "/s", "/c", "call", "./scripts/launch_codex_app_tools_mcp.cmd", "./server.mjs"]
```

The user supplied the repair transcript showing the old path and this edit. A subsequent independent filesystem/configuration check confirmed:

- `codex_app` is enabled and now points to `0.1.5`.
- The plugin cache contains only version `0.1.5`; `0.1.4` is absent.
- Both `scripts/launch_codex_app_tools_mcp.cmd` and `server.mjs` exist in `0.1.5`.
- The configuration parses successfully.

The repair transcript also reports that `codex mcp list` reads the corrected entry. That is configuration validation, **not proof of a successful MCP handshake or tool call**. No pre-fix runtime error or successful post-fix tool invocation is attached.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

The observed configuration condition is:

1. An enabled user-level `codex_app` MCP override has an absolute `cwd` pinned to plugin cache version `0.1.4`.
2. The installed cache subsequently contains only `0.1.5`.
3. The override still references `0.1.4`, leaving its configured launch directory missing.
4. Updating `cwd` to the installed version resolves the missing-path configuration defect.

The plugin update/removal sequence has not been independently replayed. We have not established which component or earlier manual setup created the override, or what removed the old directory; this report does not claim that the updater generated the stale entry.

### What is the expected behavior?

There should be a supported way to configure bundled app tools without depending on a disposable, version-specific cache path. If an explicit override targets a missing directory, surface an actionable diagnostic and the supported repair/migration path. Please clarify whether this override should instead be removed in favor of plugin-managed registration, while preserving per-tool approval settings.

A one-number manual edit can repair this instance, but it may recur if a later update removes the pinned version.

### Additional information

Related but different reports: #48314 (missing `server.mjs`) and #46598 (invalid transport). Here, the currently installed plugin has both launch files; the confirmed defect was the stale `cwd`.

A separate blank/loading desktop report is tracked in #48484. We have **not established that this MCP path defect caused or resolved that UI failure**.

Paths are redacted. No credentials, environment-variable values, private project paths, or raw logs are included.

| Native resolver starts, OS thread 1659262 | Blocking-thread queue delay: 0.109 ms |

```bash
bash reproduce-dns-guard.sh
```

Requirements: Bash, a Rust toolchain supporting edition 2024, and a native linker. Verified with Rust 1.95.0 on GNU/Linux. Cargo may download the pinned dependencies on the first build; the fixture itself opens no network sockets.

The script embeds the complete project, lockfile, licensing and source attribution. It uses the **unmodified upstream `host_resolves_to_non_public_ip` function**, its two-second deadline, and IP classifiers from 0.155.0. The guard function is also byte-for-byte identical in the checked 0.157.1 and `main` revisions.

The key sequence is:

1. Supply a simulated blocking resolver that takes 5.1 seconds and returns only `8.8.8.8:443`.
2. Call the real guard with its original two-second deadline. It returns `true` after about two seconds, the same result it uses for a non-public address.
3. Observe the blocking lookup finish after 5.1 seconds with a public address. Codex's caller maps that `true` result to `NotAllowedLocal`.

| Case | Guard result |
| --- | --- |
| Immediate public IPv4 / IPv6 | `false` |
| Public answer after 5.1 s, original 2 s deadline | `true` at 2,001 ms; public result follows at 5,100 ms |
| Public answer after 5.1 s, 10 s deadline | `false` at 5,100 ms |
| Injected resolver error | `true` |
| Private IPv4 / IPv6 or mixed public/private answers | `true` |

A DNS validation timeout or resolver error should fail the affected connection as a DNS/connectivity error. It should not claim that a private address was returned or trigger command-wide cancellation as a network-policy violation.

The validation deadline should accommodate a normal native-resolver retry. Our captured public lookup finished after approximately 5.09 seconds, beyond the current two-second deadline.

The request must remain blocked until its destination is successfully validated. Actual private-address results, including mixed public/private answers, should retain the existing policy restrictions. The application should be able to handle a transient DNS failure using its own retry logic.

- [`DNS_LOOKUP_TIMEOUT = 2 seconds`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/f0a1b8f0849d90960bc406b848f32e5a129b0457/codex-rs/network-proxy/src/runtime.rs#L50).

| Before DNS fix: injected resolver error | False private-address policy violation; command terminated |
| After fix: injected resolver error | HTTP and CONNECT both return 502; command exits normally |
| After fix: lookup exceeds ten seconds | CONNECT returns 504 after 10.004 s; command exits normally |
| After fix: lookup returns `127.0.0.1` | Existing policy denial and command termination retained |

All **293 network-proxy tests passed**, including a delayed public result and private/mixed-address controls. Scoped lint and formatting passed. items.body:
### What version of Codex CLI is running?

0.157.*

### What subscription do you have?

Plus

### Which model were you using?

_No response_

### What platform is your computer?

Linux 6.4.0-150600.23.53-64kb aarch64 aarch64

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

_No response_

### Codex doctor report

```json

```

### What issue are you seeing?

### Summary

Codex CLI fails to execute even simple shell commands such as `ls`, `pwd`, or `echo $PATH` because the Bubblewrap sandbox attempts to create a daemon socket alias under a path that is hidden by an overmount:

```text
bwrap: Can't mkdir parents for /tmp/usertmp/<username>/codex-daemon-76193: Read-only file system
```

The visible Codex daemon directory actually exists directly under:

```text
/tmp/codex-daemon-76193
```

The issue appears to be caused by Codex deriving an alternative path to the same underlying filesystem location from `/proc/self/mountinfo`, even though that alternative path is hidden by a later mount and is not reachable in the current filesystem namespace.

This occurs before the requested shell command starts.

### Environment

- Codex CLI: `0.157.1`
- Previous affected version: `0.157.0`
- OS: SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 15.6
- Architecture: `aarch64`
- Environment: shared HPC/login node
- Codex installation: standalone installer
- Bubblewrap: locally installed under `~/.local/bin`
- Codex filesystem sandbox: restricted / workspace-write
- Approval policy: `never`

`codex doctor --json` on 0.157.0 reported the standalone Linux aarch64 installation and SLES 15.6 environment. 

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Start Codex in the project directory and ask it to run a trivial command:

```text
Run ls
```

or:

```text
Run pwd
```

or:

```text
Run echo $PATH
```

The command never executes. Codex reports:

```text
bwrap: Can't mkdir parents for /tmp/usertmp/<username>/codex-daemon-76193: Read-only file system
```

### `/tmp` mount layout

The HPC has an unusual but valid stacked mount layout.

Output of:

```bash
grep -E ' /tmp |usertmp' /proc/self/mountinfo
```

is:

```text
84474 81737 259:1 / /tmp rw,nosuid,noatime master:321 - xfs /dev/nvme1n1 rw,attr2,inode64,logbufs=8,logbsize=32k,sunit=256,swidth=256,noquota
84486 84474 259:1 /usertmp /tmp/usertmp rw,nosuid,noatime master:321 - xfs /dev/nvme1n1 rw,attr2,inode64,logbufs=8,logbsize=32k,sunit=256,swidth=256,noquota
84487 84474 259:1 /usertmp/<username> /tmp rw,nosuid,noatime master:321 - xfs /dev/nvme1n1 rw,attr2,inode64,logbufs=8,logbsize=32k,sunit=256,swidth=256,noquota
84488 81741 0:25 /usertmp /dev/shm/usertmp rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec master:5 - tmpfs tmpfs rw,inode64
87376 81741 0:25 /usertmp/<username> /dev/shm rw,nosuid,nodev,noexec master:5 - tmpfs tmpfs rw,inode64
```

Output of:

```bash
findmnt -R /tmp
```

is:

```text
TARGET SOURCE               FSTYPE OPTIONS
/tmp   /dev/nvme1n1         xfs    rw,nosuid,noatime,attr2,inode64,logbufs=8,logbsize
├─/tmp/usertmp
│      /dev/nvme1n1[/usertmp]
│                           xfs    rw,nosuid,noatime,attr2,inode64,logbufs=8,logbsize
└─/tmp /dev/nvme1n1[/usertmp/<username>]
                            xfs    rw,nosuid,noatime,attr2,inode64,logbufs=8,logbsize
```

The important part is that `/tmp` is first mounted from the XFS root, but is then overmounted with:

```text
/dev/nvme1n1[/usertmp/<username>] -> /tmp
```

Therefore the visible path:

```text
/tmp/codex-daemon-76193
```

corresponds to this location on the underlying XFS filesystem:

```text
/usertmp/<username>/codex-daemon-76193
```

Through the lower `/tmp` mount, the same underlying location can also be represented as:

```text
/tmp/usertmp/<username>/codex-daemon-76193
```

However, `/tmp/usertmp` is hidden by the later `/tmp` overmount and does not exist in the filesystem namespace visible to normal processes.

For example:

```bash
ls /tmp
```

shows:

```text
codex-daemon-76193
```

but there is no visible:

```text
/tmp/usertmp
```

### What is the expected behavior?

### Expected behavior
Codex should either:

1. ignore mount aliases that are hidden by a later overmount and therefore are not reachable in the current mount namespace, or
2. avoid asking Bubblewrap to create/mask such inaccessible aliases.

For this mount layout, Codex should operate on the visible path:

```text
/tmp/codex-daemon-76193
```

without attempting to use:

```text
/tmp/usertmp/<username>/codex-daemon-76193
```

### Actual behavior

All filesystem-restricted commands fail before execution because Bubblewrap tries to create the hidden alias:

```text
bwrap: Can't mkdir parents for /tmp/usertmp/<username>/codex-daemon-76193: Read-only file system
```

### Additional diagnostic information

`codex doctor --json` on 0.157.0 reported that the app server itself was running and that the sandbox configuration was readable.

### Additional information

### `TMPDIR` workaround attempt

I also tried launching Codex with a custom temporary directory outside `/tmp`, for example:

```bash
TMPDIR=<some_local_path>/codex-tmp \
TMP=<some_local_path>/codex-tmp \
TEMP=<some_local_path>/codex-tmp \
codex
```

The environment variables are set before Codex starts.

However, Codex still uses:

```text
/tmp/codex-daemon-76193
```

for the shared daemon/socket directory, and Bubblewrap still attempts to access:

```text
/tmp/usertmp/<username>/codex-daemon-76193
```

So changing `TMPDIR` does not avoid the problematic mount-alias handling.

### Sandbox configuration

The relevant Codex configuration is approximately:

```toml
sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"
approval_policy = "never"

[permissions.workspace.filesystem]
":root" = "read"
":tmpdir" = "write"
"/tmp" = "write"

[permissions.workspace.filesystem.":project_roots"]
"." = "write"
```

Codex doctor reports the filesystem sandbox as `restricted` and shows the generated `codex-linux-sandbox` helper under `~/.codex/tmp/arg0/...`.

### Possible fix

When calculating aliases of the daemon/socket directory from `/proc/self/mountinfo`, Codex may need to account for mount visibility/overmounts.

In this case, the candidate alias:

```text
/tmp/usertmp/<username>/codex-daemon-76193
```

comes from an older/lower `/tmp` mount, but that mount is covered by:

```text
/usertmp/<username> -> /tmp
```

before the process accesses the namespace.

An alias derived from a covered mount should therefore probably not be passed to Bubblewrap as a reachable path.

"js execution timed out; kernel reset, rerun your request"

Codex ultimately reported:

"I couldn’t begin the audit: both the shell runner and the read-only desktop interface timed out before returning any system inventory."

I reproduced the shell issue afterward in a fresh Codex session using only Get-Location, so the original large prompt does not appear to be the cause.

PowerShell itself works normally outside Codex and returns commands immediately.

Additional observations:
- The problem began after updating from Codex CLI 0.154.0 to 0.157.1.
- Multiple codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe processes appeared while Codex was attempting commands.
- Additional visible Windows Terminal/console windows appeared from the Codex app-server daemon.
- `codex doctor --json` reports `sandbox provisioning: complete` with the elevated sandbox backend.
- The same doctor report reports the background app-server socket as `stale or unreachable` and says it failed to connect to the control socket.
- Codex installation is reported as consistent by `codex doctor`.
- Network/WebSocket connectivity checks in `codex doctor` succeed.

No system modifications are required to reproduce the issue.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Install/update Codex CLI to 0.157.1 on Windows 11.

2. Open Windows Terminal with PowerShell 7.

3. Start Codex normally:

   codex

4. Start a fresh thread/session.

5. Enter the following prompt:

   Run Get-Location. Nothing else.

6. Codex attempts to execute the PowerShell command but the command runner does not return.

7. After approximately 3 minutes, Codex terminates the attempt and reports:

   "Get-Location did not return; the command stalled and was terminated."

Expected behavior:
Get-Location should execute immediately and return the current working directory.

Actual behavior:
The Codex command runner hangs for several minutes and eventually terminates the command.

Control test:
Running the following directly in the same PowerShell environment outside Codex works immediately:

Get-Location

The issue also reproduces with larger read-only tasks, but Get-Location is the smallest reproduction I have found.

During affected sessions I have also observed multiple codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe processes and visible console windows associated with the app-server daemon.

`codex doctor --json` reports:
- Codex CLI 0.157.1
- Windows x86_64
- installation looks consistent
- sandbox backend: elevated
- sandbox provisioning: complete
- background app-server socket: stale or unreachable
- app-server version unavailable because connection to the control socket failed

Thread ID:
Not applicable / fresh CLI thread.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex should execute the requested shell command normally and return its output without hanging.

For the minimal reproduction, `Get-Location` should complete almost immediately and return the current working directory.

More generally, Codex should be able to execute shell commands so it can proceed with the task requested by the user.

### Additional information

The issue started immediately after updating Codex CLI from 0.154.0 to 0.157.1.

While reproducing the issue, I noticed:
- Multiple `codex-windows-sandbox-setup.exe` processes running concurrently.
- Visible console/Windows Terminal windows being spawned by the Codex app-server daemon.
- `codex doctor --json` reports the sandbox as successfully provisioned (`sandbox provisioning: complete`, backend `elevated`).
- The same doctor report reports the background app-server socket as `stale or unreachable` and cannot retrieve the app-server version because it fails to connect to the control socket.
- Codex reports its installation as consistent.
- Codex network and WebSocket connectivity checks succeed.
- PowerShell commands execute normally when run directly outside Codex.

I first encountered this during a read-only filesystem/storage audit, but reproduced it afterward in a fresh Codex session using only `Get-Location`, so the original task does not appear to be responsible.

I have attached/provided the redacted `codex doctor --json` output with this report.

codex-cli 0.157.1

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro

GPT-6-Astra

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What terminal emulator and version are you using (if applicable)?

PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7

### Codex doctor report

```json

```

### What issue are you seeing?

## Summary

In normal daemon mode, Codex CLI displays a Git-parent trust warning for an empty non-Git folder. The current directory and alleged repository root identify the same Windows directory, differing only in letter case. This is misleading at a security-sensitive consent boundary.

> Note: This was tested both elevated and non-elevated. A detailed example is shown but can also be easily reproduced by simply opening PowerShell (5.1/7.x) and typing codex. The message appears even when the current directory is the users home directory, which has no git.

## Environment

- Windows, unelevated PowerShell process (token checked).
- Tested executable: `C:\Users\user01\AppData\Local\Programs\OpenAI\Codex\bin\codex.exe`
- CLI version: `codex-cli 0.157.1`.
- Test folder: `C:\Users\user01\AppData\Local\Temp\CodexTrustRepro-20260927\plain`.
- No `.git` or `.lore` markers found in the test folder or any ancestor through `C:\`.
- No Unreal process or project content is required for this reproduction.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

## Reproduction

Use a new, untrusted directory outside any repository. Run from ordinary PowerShell:

```powershell
$testFolder = Join-Path ([IO.Path]::GetTempPath()) ('CodexTrustRepro-' + [guid]::NewGuid().ToString('N') + '\plain')
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $testFolder | Out-Null
$cliPath = Join-Path $env:LOCALAPPDATA 'Programs\OpenAI\Codex\bin\codex.exe'
& $cliPath --no-alt-screen -C $testFolder
```

Inspect the folder-trust screen without accepting trust. Escape returns to Agent Command Center; Ctrl+C exits the client. Do not stop the shared daemon.

Repeat against the SAME untrusted folder:

```powershell
& $cliPath --no-daemon --no-alt-screen -C $testFolder
& $cliPath --no-alt-screen -C $testFolder.ToLowerInvariant()
```

Dismiss each prompt before starting the next comparison. The lowercase-path comparison is for a conventional case-insensitive Windows folder; it is diagnostic, not a proposed general-purpose path conversion.

## Observed results

| Invocation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Normal daemon mode, mixed-case path | Incorrect Git-subdirectory warning |
| `--no-daemon`, mixed-case path | Folder-only trust prompt, no Git warning |
| Normal daemon mode, lowercase path | Folder-only trust prompt, no Git warning |

Normal mode displayed:

```text
Folder access
C:\Users\user01\AppData\Local\Temp\CodexTrustRepro-20260927\plain

Note: You’re in a subdirectory of a Git project. Trusting will apply to the
repository root:
c:\users\user01\appdata\local\temp\codextrustrepro-20260927\plain
```

All three cases still asked the user whether to trust the folder. No prompt was accepted and no model task was submitted.

The user configuration SHA-256 was identical before and after the two daemon-mode comparisons.
No trust entry containing `codextrustrepro` was present afterward. The hash baseline was taken after the initial no-daemon test, not before the entire investigation.

### What is the expected behavior?

## Expected behavior

- Display the actual trust target accurately.
- Do not describe equivalent Windows paths as a parent/child relationship merely because their casing differs.
- Mention Git only when Git repository discovery actually establishes a repository.
- If trust truly applies to a parent, display that distinct parent explicitly.
- Keep user consent; do not suppress the trust prompt to fix its wording.

## Interpretation and limits

The results strongly suggest a case-normalization mismatch between the client and shared-daemon trust metadata. This is a hypothesis, not a source-code-confirmed root cause. The incorrect Git label may be a separate overly broad UI condition.

These tests demonstrate incorrect wording. They do not demonstrate unintended parent-directory trust: no trust was accepted, and the displayed paths referred to the same directory.

### Additional information

Reproduces on this Windows system with Codex CLI 0.157.1 in shared-daemon mode, including in an empty non-Git directory. Independent confirmation on another Windows system is requested.

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex desktop app, connected to a remote Linux workspace. Desktop build number was not collected for this usability report.

## Context

Make the **modified hooks / review before trusting** interface provide enough information for an informed approval: a change comparison, accessible source, and an explanation of possible effects.

The composer indicated that two hooks had been modified and needed review. In the review view, the visible/copied details were Source, Hook type, Command, Matcher, and Timeout. The entries were a `PreToolUse` hook matching `Bash` and a `UserPromptSubmit` hook. Their commands invoked wrapper scripts and other scripts.

From this view I could tell when a command would run, but could not find:

- What changed since the version I previously trusted.
- The contents of the scripts behind the displayed command, or an obvious way to inspect them from the review.
- What the hook can actually do when it fires: block a command, add instructions, modify input, or perform other script side effects; or what happens if the hook fails.

An agent could explain the current behavior only after separately reading the scripts. For example, one returned an explicit denial to block a pending shell command, while the other added email-writing instructions. Those are materially different effects, but the displayed event/command metadata did not communicate them. The exact change from the previously trusted version was still unresolved.

## Scope

One coherent improvement to the evidence available in the modified-hook review flow:

1. Show the **previously approved definition versus the current definition**, highlighting the fields that changed. If the previous version was not retained, say so explicitly instead of implying a comparison is available.
2. Provide **open source / inspect referenced script** actions. Make clear what trust covers (definition, command text, script contents, etc.). If script snapshots are retained, offer their comparison; otherwise identify that limitation.
3. Explain the **possible outcomes of the event** and provide a clearly attributed behavior summary for the particular hook. Distinguish declared or agent-inferred behavior from behavior verified by checks; do not imply arbitrary scripts can be fully understood from their names. This must not execute or trust a hook just to inspect it.

The human trust boundary is useful. The problem is being asked to make that decision with information that describes invocation but not the change or consequences. The result is an interruption that requires a separate technical investigation before the user can proceed confidently.

## Acceptance

From a pending modified-hook entry, a user can inspect the change or see an explicit unavailable-baseline notice, open the relevant source, and understand the possible outcomes and scope of trust before deciding. Inspecting these details does not itself execute or trust the hook.

### Additional information

This reports the user's observed panel and copied fields, plus separate source inspection; it is not an exhaustive audit of every UI path or desktop build. No hook was trusted as part of this investigation. No private paths, project details, configuration contents, or session logs are attached.

## References

- [Official hook documentation: review and trust](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks#review-and-trust-hooks) describes exact-definition trust; the PreToolUse section documents denial and additional-context outcomes.
- [Official desktop feedback route](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/reference/troubleshooting#feedback-and-logs).
- Related: #47285 concerns the scope of per-hook versus bulk approval. This request concerns the evidence and explanations available **before** approval.

No release milestone requested: this is an upstream desktop usability improvement, not a commitment to a particular release.

### What version of Codex CLI is running?

`codex-cli 0.157.0`

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 (build 26200), native CLI, `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"`, `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"`.

### What issue are you seeing?

Two lasting filesystem side effects from the elevated Windows sandbox:

1. **ACEs are added and never removed.** For each writable root (cwd and `--add-dir`), setup grants inheritable Modify-style allow ACEs to `CodexSandboxUsers` and a per-root capability SID, and deny ACEs for that capability SID on `.git` / `.agents` (including `.git\worktrees\<name>` when that is the workspace). Those entries remain after the run ends, after a kill, and (from what we can tell) after uninstall. Over normal use they accumulate across projects, `%TEMP%`, profile paths touched as roots, etc., and show up as unresolved capability SIDs in the ACL UI.

2. **Sandbox-owned owner-only directories lock out the interactive user.** Commands run as `CodexSandboxOffline` / `CodexSandboxOnline`, so new files are owned by that account. On Python 3.13+, `os.mkdir(..., 0o700)` / pytest `--basetemp` / `tmp_path` write a protected DACL (owner / SYSTEM / Administrators only). The interactive user then cannot list, `icacls /reset`, or delete those trees without an elevated `takeown`. This is the host-user counterpart of the in-sandbox 0o700 failures.

Separately: the deny ACE on a worktree gitdir prevents the sandbox from creating `.git/index.lock` there (user write still works).

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Set `[windows] sandbox = "elevated"` and `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"`.
2. Snapshot ACLs: `icacls <dir> /save before.txt /t`.
3. `codex exec -s workspace-write --cd <dir> "run: python -c \"import os; os.mkdir('locked', 0o700)\""` (Python 3.13+).
4. `icacls <dir>` — new `CodexSandboxUsers` + capability SID ACEs remain after the process exits.
5. As the normal user: `dir <dir>\locked` and `icacls <dir>\locked /reset` → Access is denied.
6. Optional A/B: `[windows] sandbox = "mxc"` on a PSEC-capable host — no ACL mutation; `locked` owned by the user and readable.

### What is the expected behavior?

- ACEs Codex adds for a run are removed when the run ends (or reconciled on next start after a crash), **or** a documented `codex sandbox cleanup` removes every ACE / capability mapping Codex created.
- Files created in the sandbox remain controllable by the invoking user (ownership and/or inherited ACEs that include the user), including Python 0o700 temps.
- Uninstall reverses setup grants.
- Where MXC is available, prefer it (or document it) as the Windows backend that confines writes **without** rewriting host DACLs.

### Additional information

Related (not the same ask):

- #41169 — capability SIDs accumulate; no cleanup lifecycle (closest on leftover ACEs).
- #17179 / #29867 — workspace/subtree left owned by `CodexSandbox*`.
- #19791 — 0o700 temps inaccessible *inside* the sandbox.
- #29415 — policy to disable ACL mutation (prevention, not cleanup).
- #13378 — ACL setup / home pollution.

This issue is specifically: **missing cleanup of added ACEs**, **host-user lockout from sandbox-owned 0o700 trees**, and **MXC as a non-ACL backend** where supported.

items.body:
# macOS Computer Use: ~27 GiB of WindowServer capture surfaces remain mapped after hours of RDP control

## Summary

After I used Codex Computer Use to control an RDP session for several hours, macOS continued reporting roughly 28 GB for `WindowServer`. The Computer Use task had finished when I noticed the retained memory.

Live diagnostics found **3,405 distinct WindowServer capture surfaces mapped in `SkyComputerUseService`, totaling 29,021,749,248 bytes (27.029 GiB)**. Of these, 3,402 are 1924 × 1090 BGRA surfaces of 8,320 KiB each. Their owner label is `SL.426:CaptureSurface`, matching the live WindowServer PID, 426.

Computer History was also running in the same service. The evidence identifies retained capture storage in the Computer Use service; the specific consumer and underlying cleanup defect still need investigation.

## Environment

- macOS 27.0, build `26A428`, arm64
- Apple M4, model `Mac16,13`, **24 GiB physical unified memory**
- Built-in display only: 2880 × 1864 Retina
- ChatGPT desktop hosting Codex: `26.924.22138`, build `11645`, bundle `com.openai.codex`
- Computer Use helper: `26.923.1001242`, build `1001242`, bundle `com.openai.sky.CUAService`
- Bundled Codex CLI: `0.158.0-alpha.2.1`
- Observation: September 27, 2026, approximately 18:26–18:29 CEST
- Desktop process and Computer Use service had been running since approximately 12:37 CEST
- Computer History status: `running`, started at `2026-09-27T10:37:36Z`

## Observed sequence

1. I used native Computer Use to control an RDP session over several hours.
2. The Computer Use task ended. I left the desktop app open; Computer History remained enabled.
3. The large WindowServer memory reading persisted after the task ended.
4. Read-only diagnostics showed the capture surfaces below. Repeated snapshots over approximately three minutes showed the same 3,469 total IOSurface mappings and roughly 27 GiB of IOSurface storage in the helper.

This is an observed incident, not yet a minimal deterministic reproduction. The exact RDP action that causes retention has not been isolated.

## Diagnostic evidence

The service was PID `36787`, a direct child of the desktop app PID `36628`. WindowServer was PID `426`.

`top` reported:

```text
PID    COMMAND              MEM    CMPRS
426    WindowServer         28G    406M
36787  SkyComputerUseSe     115M   27G
```

`vmmap -summary 36787` reported:

```text
Physical footprint:         115.0M
Physical footprint (peak):  793.3M

REGION TYPE                 VIRTUAL SIZE    REGION COUNT
IOSurface                   27.0G           3469
```

The full `vmmap` contained 3,405 distinct capture `SurfaceID` values, for example:

```text
IOSurface [8320K 0K 0K 0K] rw-/rw- SM=SHM PURGE=N
SurfaceID: 0x22a  1924x1090 (BGRA) 8320K  'SL.426:CaptureSurface'
```

Capture-surface breakdown:

| Dimensions | Count |
| --- | ---: |
| 1924 × 1090 BGRA | 3,402 |
| 1920 × 1080 BGRA | 1 |
| 2560 × 1440 BGRA | 2 |

`footprint --swapped --vmObjectDirty -p 36787` accounted for the shared backing storage:

```text
VM Object Dirty Analysis: Enabled
SkyComputerUseService [36787]: Footprint: 27 GB

Dirty     (Swapped)    Regions    Category
27 GB     27 GB        3469       IOSurface

Auxiliary data:
phys_footprint: 115 MB
phys_footprint_peak: 793 MB
```

Default process footprint accounting reports approximately 115 MB for the helper, while VM-object accounting exposes its mapped shared capture storage. A plain RSS or helper-footprint check therefore misses the scale of this incident. The WindowServer and helper readings refer to shared storage and should not be summed as independent allocations.

System snapshots reported approximately 22–23 GiB used physical memory, approximately 10–11 GiB in the physical compressor, and `329.75M` swap usage. Compressed logical bytes and shared allocation accounting explain how the displayed process value can exceed the machine's installed RAM.

## Expected behavior

Capture buffers should have a bounded lifetime. After an RDP Computer Use task ends, thousands of old capture surfaces should not remain retained in the service. An enabled background Computer History recorder should also keep its capture-buffer use bounded.

Please investigate capture-surface ownership and release across native Computer Use, RDP-window captures, Computer History, and task/client teardown.

## Limits and related reports

- No baseline before RDP use or continuous memory-growth trace was captured.
- No helper restart, desktop-app restart, or Computer History pause was performed, so release on teardown has not yet been verified.
- It remains unresolved whether retention is in Codex's consumer/lifecycle code or an interaction with the macOS capture APIs.
- #35659 reports a ScreenCaptureKit stream continuing after Computer Use ends.
- #37062 reports WindowServer failures in the capture/IOSurface path.
- A shared root cause with those reports has not been established; this report adds quantified retained capture-memory evidence on a newer app/helper version.

Only selected technical diagnostics are included here. Screenshots, session transcripts, RDP endpoint details, and raw desktop logs are omitted.

items.title: [ChatGPT Web][Sep 2026 UI] Conversation workflow regressions: native links/new-tab behavior removed and direct Delete action lost

labels.name: bug

items.body:
### Summary

The recent ChatGPT web UI update introduced several related conversation-navigation and lifecycle regressions on `chatgpt.com`.

These are not requests for new advanced features. They are previously available browser/UI workflows that disappeared with the new interface.

The regressions I can reproduce are:

1. **“New chat” no longer behaves like a normal browser link.**
2. **Existing conversation entries no longer behave like normal browser links.**
3. As a consequence, standard browser actions are lost:
   - Right-click → **Open link in new tab**
   - **Ctrl+Click**
   - **Middle-click**
   - **Copy link address**
4. **Delete has been removed from the menu of the currently open conversation**, forcing the user to find the same conversation again in the sidebar/search before it can be deleted.

These changes all move conversation management away from direct/native browser interaction and toward extra sidebar/search navigation.

### Environment

- Surface: `chatgpt.com`
- OS: Windows 11
- Browser: Microsoft Edge
- First observed: immediately after the September 25, 2026 ChatGPT web UI update
- Reproduced again on September 27, 2026

### Regression 1 — New chat can no longer be opened directly in a new tab

Previously, “New chat” behaved like a link.

Expected browser workflows included:

- Right-click → Open link in new tab
- Ctrl+Click
- Middle-click

With the current UI, right-clicking “New chat” produces the generic page context menu rather than a link context menu.

This means a user who wants to preserve the current conversation and start another one in parallel now has to:

```
open another browser tab
→ navigate to ChatGPT
→ start a new chat there
```

instead of simply opening “New chat” in another tab.

### Regression 2 — Existing conversations no longer preserve native link behavior

The same problem affects conversation entries.

When conversation entries are not real links, standard browser navigation is lost:

- no native Open in new tab
- no Ctrl+Click
- no middle-click
- no Copy link address

This is especially disruptive for workflows where several conversations are used in parallel and compared against each other.

### Regression 3 — Browser-native context-menu functionality has been removed

The practical issue is not only the absence of an explicit “Open in new tab” button.

The new UI removes normal browser link semantics entirely.

That means the browser can no longer provide functionality it already knows how to provide for free.

This is a regression from normal web behavior and makes ChatGPT navigation less interoperable with the browser.

### Regression 4 — Delete is no longer available from the currently open conversation

Before the UI update, the menu of the currently open conversation included **Delete**.

The previous workflow was:

```
open chat
→ use chat
→ decide whether it is worth keeping
→ delete it immediately from the currently open conversation
```

The current workflow is:

```
open chat
→ use chat
→ decide it is not worth keeping
→ leave the current context
→ find the same chat again in the sidebar or search
→ open another menu
→ delete it there
```

During the rollout I also observed inconsistent behavior inside the same account: an older existing chat still exposed the direct Delete action while a chat using the current UI did not.

Temporary Chat is not an equivalent workaround because the user often does not know at the beginning of a conversation whether the conversation will be worth keeping.

### Why these regressions matter together

These changes all increase navigation and context-switching overhead.

For intensive technical/development use, parallel ChatGPT tabs are not cosmetic. They are used to:

- preserve one conversation while starting another task;
- compare outputs between conversations;
- inspect previous project context;
- supervise coding/agent work in parallel;
- keep long-running technical threads available without repeatedly searching for them.

The removal of native link behavior forces additional navigation every time a parallel conversation is needed.

The removal of direct Delete forces the user to search for a conversation that is already open in front of them.

This also discourages cleanup: chats remain in history not because the user wants to keep them, but because deleting them now requires extra search/navigation work.

### Cost / supervision impact

For coding-heavy use, model and agent usage is metered and valuable enough that users cannot simply ignore efficiency, leave everything running indefinitely, and rerun work whenever something goes wrong.

Active human supervision, context preservation, and comparison between threads are part of the real cost of using the product.

A UI change that repeatedly adds navigation, searching, and context switching therefore increases the human supervision cost of the product even if each individual interaction only adds a few seconds.

Repeated across a development day, that becomes significant.

### Steps to reproduce

#### Native-link / new-tab regression

1. Open `https://chatgpt.com/` in Microsoft Edge on Windows 11.
2. Right-click **New chat** in the sidebar.
3. Observe that the browser shows the generic page context menu rather than a link context menu.
4. Try Ctrl+Click or middle-click on **New chat**.
5. Observe that it does not provide the previous native new-tab workflow.
6. Repeat with an existing conversation entry.

#### Direct Delete regression

1. Open a normal ChatGPT conversation.
2. Open the three-dot menu for the currently open conversation.
3. Observe that **Delete** is not available there in the current UI.
4. To delete the conversation, go to the sidebar/search.
5. Find the same conversation again.
6. Open its sidebar menu.
7. Delete it there.

### Expected behavior

ChatGPT should preserve standard browser navigation semantics.

Preferred behavior:

- “New chat” is a real link/deep link where technically possible.
- Conversation entries are real links/deep links.
- Right-click, Ctrl+Click, and middle-click work normally.
- Copy link address is available.
- The currently open conversation includes a direct Delete action with the existing confirmation dialog.

If ChatGPT requires custom JavaScript navigation internally, an equivalent explicit **Open in new tab** action should be provided without removing native browser behavior where possible.

### Actual behavior

The current UI replaces direct/native workflows with additional in-app navigation:

- New chat cannot be opened in another tab using normal browser link behavior.
- Existing conversation entries lose native link actions.
- Standard right-click/Ctrl+Click/middle-click workflows are removed.
- Deleting the currently open conversation requires finding the conversation again in the sidebar/search.

### Scope

I am grouping these together because they appeared with the same recent web UI change and they have the same user-facing effect: conversation navigation and lifecycle management now require more in-app searching and context switching.

If these are owned by different internal components, please split them internally as needed, but they represent one coherent workflow regression from the user side.

### Related community reports

Similar regressions are already being discussed in the OpenAI Developer Community, including reports about:

- conversations no longer being normal links;

In a user-opened IAB tab, Browser Use intermittently fails to activate visible, enabled page controls with pointer-based clicks. 2. Attempt to activate an editor's “Code View” toolbar button using a Playwright locator click, an accessibility click, and a coordinate click. Repeated attempts do not toggle the mode; the toolbar may lose focus or hide.

labels.name: bug
